topics.title: GOC Standards for Optical Students
topics.summary: The General Optical Council (GOC) regulates optometrists, dispensing opticians and students in training. As a registered student you're expected to meet the GOC's Standards for Optical Students: putting patients first, communicating well, getting consent, working within your competence, being honest, and behaving professionally — in and out of clinic, including online.
keyPoints: Optometry students in the UK must be registered with the GOC while training.
The Standards for Optical Students set out the behaviour expected; they mirror the Standards of Practice for registrants.

Themes include: listening to patients and putting them first, communicating effectively, obtaining valid consent, showing care and respect, protecting confidentiality, working within your competence and under supervision.
Also: being honest and trustworthy, being candid when things go wrong, raising concerns about patient safety, and maintaining public confidence in the profession.
Professional behaviour applies outside clinic too — including social media.
Concerns about a student's fitness to train can be raised with the university and the GOC.
Check optical.org for the current version (new standards came into effect from January 2025).
examTraps: Thinking the standards only apply in clinic.
Forgetting that students must be GOC-registered.
Quoting old wording — always refer to the current version.

diagram.description: A circle labelled 'The patient' in the centre, surrounded by segments: communication, consent, care and respect, confidentiality, competence and supervision, honesty and candour, raising concerns, professionalism (including online).

goDeeper.heading: Working within your competence
goDeeper.body: As a student you work under supervision. Know what you're allowed to do, ask when unsure, never present yourself as qualified, and make sure patients know you're a student. If something is beyond you, stop and get your supervisor — that's professional, not a weakness.

goDeeper.heading: Social media and conduct
goDeeper.body: Don't post about patients (even 'anonymised' stories can identify people), don't share clinic photos with patient information, and think about how posts reflect on the profession. Conduct outside clinic — including academic honesty — counts towards fitness to train.

flashcards.front: Who regulates optometry students in the UK?

flashcards.back: Yes — with the GOC, while training.
Yes — professional behaviour includes social media.

flashcards.front: Where to find the current standards

mcq.q: A classmate posts a funny story about a clinic patient without their name. What's the issue?

options.text: It may still identify the patient and breaches confidentiality and professionalism
options.feedback: Yes — details can identify people, and it undermines trust.

options.text: No issue — no name was used
options.feedback: Other details can still identify someone.

options.text: Only an issue if the patient sees it
options.feedback: The breach happens when it's posted.
They do — there are specific Standards for Optical Students.

mcq.explanation: Confidentiality and professional conduct apply online and offline; 'anonymised' stories can still identify patients.

topics.title: Communication and consent
topics.summary: Valid consent must be voluntary, informed and given by someone with capacity. Good communication makes consent meaningful: explain what you'll do and why, check understanding, and respect the answer.
keyPoints: Valid consent: voluntary (no pressure), informed (benefits, risks, alternatives), and the person has capacity.
Consent can be verbal, written or implied — but implied consent shouldn't be assumed for anything invasive (e.g. drops, contact tonometry).

Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England & Wales): assume capacity unless shown otherwise; a person lacks capacity for a decision if they can't understand, retain, use/weigh the information, or communicate a decision.
Children: parental consent, or the child's own consent if Gillick competent.
Consent is specific and ongoing — patients can withdraw at any time.
Communication skills: open questions, active listening, no jargon, check understanding (teach-back), non-verbal cues, interpreters when needed.
Record consent and important information given.
examTraps: Assuming a signature equals informed consent.
Using a family member as an interpreter for sensitive information without thought.

diagram.description: Triangle with three corners: voluntary, informed, capacity — 'valid consent' in the centre. Under 'capacity', four boxes: understand, retain, use/weigh, communicate.

goDeeper.heading: Consent for eye drops
goDeeper.body: Before dilating: explain why, the effects (blur, light sensitivity, not driving until vision is clear), rare risks (e.g. angle closure symptoms to watch for), and alternatives. Ask if they have questions, check they agree, and record it. If they decline, record that and the implications you explained.

goDeeper.heading: Teach-back
goDeeper.body: Instead of 'Do you understand?', ask 'Just so I know I've explained it well, can you tell me what you'll do if your eye gets red and painful?' It checks understanding without making the patient feel tested.

goDeeper.heading: Across the UK
goDeeper.body: Capacity law differs between nations (e.g. the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 in Scotland). The principles — presume capacity, support decision-making, act in the person's best interests when they lack capacity — are similar.

flashcards.back: A child with enough understanding and maturity can consent for themselves.
Asking the patient to explain back in their own words to check understanding.

mcq.q: A patient agrees to drops after you say 'I'm just going to put some drops in'. Is this valid consent?

options.text: No — they weren't informed of purpose, effects and risks
options.feedback: Right — consent must be informed.
Not objecting isn't informed consent.
They do.

options.text: Only if they sign a form
options.feedback: Verbal consent can be valid if it's informed.

mcq.explanation: Patients need to know why, what to expect and the risks before they can give valid consent.

topics.title: Interprofessional learning (IPL)
topics.summary: Interprofessional learning brings students from different health professions together to learn with, from and about each other, so they can work better as teams and improve patient care. Your IPL session is compulsory.
keyPoints: Definition (CAIPE): when two or more professions learn with, from and about each other to improve collaboration and the quality of care.
Your IPL session: Thu 19 Nov, 14:00–16:00 (rooms G77/79/81) — compulsory.
Know other eye-care roles: dispensing opticians, orthoptists, ophthalmologists, ophthalmic nurses, GPs, pharmacists.
Optometrists often refer to and work alongside GPs, pharmacists and hospital eye services.
Clear communication between professions (e.g. SBAR: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) reduces errors.
Respect for each profession's expertise and scope is central to good teamwork.
Reflect on what you learned about other roles and how it changes your practice.
examTraps: Treating IPL as just 'meeting other students' rather than learning about roles and teamwork.
Not knowing what orthoptists and dispensing opticians do.

diagram.description: A patient in the centre connected to: optometrist, dispensing optician, orthoptist, ophthalmologist, GP, pharmacist, ophthalmic nurse — with arrows showing typical referral and communication routes.

goDeeper.heading: SBAR in eye care
goDeeper.body: Situation: 'I'm calling about Mrs X, who has a painful red eye and reduced vision.' Background: 'She wears monthly contact lenses and slept in them.' Assessment: 'There's a 2 mm central infiltrate with an epithelial defect — I suspect microbial keratitis.' Recommendation: 'Could she be seen in eye casualty today?' Clear and quick for the person receiving it.

goDeeper.heading: Who does what
goDeeper.body: Dispensing opticians fit and dispense spectacles (and with extra qualification, contact lenses). Orthoptists specialise in binocular vision and eye movement disorders (e.g. amblyopia treatment). Ophthalmologists are medical doctors specialising in eye disease and surgery. Pharmacists advise on medicines, including eye drops and side effects.

flashcards.back: Two or more professions learning with, from and about each other to improve collaboration and care.
Binocular vision and eye movement disorders.

mcq.q: Which professional mainly manages amblyopia treatment programmes in UK hospitals?

options.feedback: Yes — alongside ophthalmologists.
They dispense spectacles.
They advise on medicines.
GPs refer but don't manage amblyopia treatment.

mcq.explanation: Orthoptists specialise in binocular vision and run amblyopia treatment within hospital eye services.

topics.askClaude: Help me practise SBAR: give me 3 eye scenarios and let me phone through a referral to you as the receiving doctor, then give feedback.

topics.title: Reflective practice
topics.summary: From the week 3 PPD lecture: reflection turns experience into learning. The GOC expects critical reflection throughout your career, so know the models, what good academic reflective writing looks like, and how to write a CPD reflection.
keyPoints: GOC definition (CPD guide, 2024): thinking analytically about your experiences to gain insight and improve the way you work and the care you give. Linked to GOC outcomes 7.4 and 5.1.
Critical reflection moves from describing to analysing: evaluate current practice, consider what's desirable and what's possible, and form new understanding that changes what you do.
Models: Driscoll (2000) / Rolfe et al. (2001), 'What? So what? Now what?', and Gibbs' reflective cycle (1988): description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan.

Academic reflective writing isn't just description, a diary, self-disclosure, flattery of the course or uncritical referencing. It needs structure, formal language and evidence of learning and how you'll use it.
Benefits: embeds good practice, improves quality of care and assures the public.
CPD reflections: what you expected, what you learned, and whether and how you'll apply it. Anonymise: nothing that identifies a patient or practitioner.
Prompt questions: what happened, key takeaways, how issues were addressed, what you'd do differently, the impact, quick changes and longer-term gaps.
examTraps: Writing a reflection that only describes what happened.
Including details that could identify a patient or colleague.

diagram.description: Circular diagram with six stages and arrows: Description, Feelings, Evaluation, Analysis, Conclusion, Action plan, returning to Description.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: other models
goDeeper.body: Kolb's cycle (experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, active experimentation) and Schön's reflection-in-action (during) versus reflection-on-action (after). Making your action plan SMART (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound) keeps it concrete.

flashcards.back: Description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan.
In-action = during the event; on-action = afterwards (Schön).
It moves from describing an experience to analysing it in a systematic way, to find what was good and what could improve.

mcq.q: Which stage of Gibbs' cycle asks 'why did it happen?' and links to theory?

options.feedback: Yes — making sense of the situation.
That's what happened.
That's what you thought and felt.
That's what you'll do next time.

mcq.explanation: Analysis is where you explore causes and connect the experience to knowledge and theory.

mcq.q: Which of these best fits good academic reflective writing?

options.text: A structured account that uses the experience to show what you learned and how you will use it
options.feedback: Yes. Description is only the starting point; you evidence the learning and the next step.

options.text: A detailed description of exactly what happened
options.feedback: Description alone is the commonest mistake. It should be the foundation for learning, not the whole piece.

options.text: A private diary in any language you like
options.feedback: Academic reflection needs structure and formal language, and must suit the reader.

options.text: As much personal disclosure as possible
options.feedback: You don't get marks for self-disclosure. Experiences must be used actively to promote learning.

mcq.explanation: The lecture lists what reflective writing is not: plain description, a diary, self-disclosure, flattery of the course, or uncritical referencing.

topics.askClaude: Help me write a short Gibbs reflection on a clinic or lab experience I'll describe. Ask me questions for each stage rather than writing it for me.
